children: China is hitting the brakes on the wave of humanoid-robot makers seeking to go public, people familiar with the matter told Reuters, as regulators weigh if these companies' revenues reflect commercial demand.
Chinese regulators have used informal "window guidance" to hold back some of these companies' listings, according to the sources.
One source said humanoid robot IPOs were effectively frozen for now. Another said there was no formal ban, but rather a sector-specific slowdown.
The main concern is whether revenue generated by these companies through local government-backed projects can be sustained.
Robot training centers and joint ventures, in which local governments could provide 80%-90% of the initial investment, generated significant revenue for some companies.

While such projects can help companies meet listing thresholds, regulators are questioning whether they represent demand from independent customers. Valuations for some robot firms could fall 60%-70% if revenues linked to such projects are stripped away.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission recently gave informal guidance to some investment firms that it was raising the bar for approving humanoid robot IPOs,
reported previously, citing people with knowledge of ⁠the matter.
At least half a dozen Chinese humanoid robot makers are planning to go ​public, including Deep Robotics, X Square Robot and AGIBOT.

The regulatory move points to China's effort to cool investor euphoria over humanoid robots, especially since Unitree Robotics' IPO, in which its shares surged more than fivefold but have since slumped 55% from their peak.

title: Chinese regulators slow humanoid robot IPO wave - report
